conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood. Today we’ll use a short tool called the EPDS—it’s a 10-question screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. It’s not a test of “good” or “bad” mothering; it just gives us a snapshot of how you’re coping so we can make sure you have the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go at your pace, and you can pause any time. Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh, eyes on the baby blanket in my lap]

It’s been… pretty hard. Most of the time nothing feels funny, and when my husband tries to joke—he used to make me laugh so easily—I just kind of force a smile so he won’t worry. I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed for real.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[gives a small shake of the head]  

Not really. I mean, maybe once or twice a tiny giggle slipped out when the baby made a silly face, but it disappeared as fast as it came. Mostly it feels like I’m too tired and heavy inside to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

I still look forward to my morning coffee and sometimes to the short walk we take to the mailbox, but that’s about it. Things I used to get excited about—like meeting friends or ordering take-out with my husband—just feel like chores now. I’ll think “I should enjoy this,” but the happy feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor, voice tight]

Yeah... more often than I want to admit. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to "I'm doing something wrong." The other night he wouldn't settle after a feeding and I kept replaying everything—did I eat something that hurt his stomach, am I holding him wrong, maybe I'm just not cut out for this. Rationally I know babies cry, but the guilt still sneaks in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, rocking the baby a little tighter]

Pretty much every day. I'll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds off, or I'll imagine him slipping out of my arms if I stand up too fast. There's no real reason—he's healthy, the pediatrician says everything looks great—but the thoughts just pop in and keep looping. Sometimes I can take a few breaths and calm down, other times it sticks with me for hours.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings the edge of the blanket]

A couple of times, yeah. Yesterday the baby was napping and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get air. Nothing had happened—no noise, no bad dream—it just hit. It passed after a minute, but I sat there shaking, watching the monitor like something awful was about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, laundry—three more pile up. I’ll look around the living room and just feel… swallowed. Some mornings I lie there after the baby’s 4 a.m. feed thinking, “How am I going to get through today?” I haven’t had anything to drink or take, but the weight of it all makes me want to hide under the covers.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[lightly rubs her eyes]

Yeah… Once I finally lie down, my mind won’t quit running through all the “what-ifs.” I replay every little cry or grunt he made, wonder if I burped him long enough, if the swaddle’s too tight. It takes me forever to drift off, and then I jolt awake at least once or twice sure I heard him when he’s still sound asleep. I end up staring at the ceiling feeling this heavy sadness until the next feeding.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes glassy]

Most of the day, almost every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud parked over me. I’ll be holding him and still feel this ache in my chest. Sometimes I’ll catch myself just staring off, feeling empty even when he’s smiling up at me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, voice cracks]

Yeah… a couple times this week. Yesterday I couldn’t get him to latch, and after the third try I just started bawling. My husband found me in the nursery with tears dripping on the nursing pillow. It’s not like me—I never used to cry much—but the sadness just bubbles over before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[quiet for a long moment, eyes fixed on the baby]

Once or twice, in a… fleeting way. Nothing planned—just this flash of “what if I weren’t here.” It scared me enough that I hugged him tighter and pushed it away. I don’t want to leave him; I just want the heaviness to stop.

You have shared that the past weeks have felt overwhelmingly heavy-laughter and excitement rarely reach you, guilt and self-criticism surface many times a day, and a constant gray cloud of sadness leaves you teary and exhausted. Moments of sudden panic, racing thoughts at night, and feeling swallowed by even simple tasks show how hard you are working to keep your head above water while loving and protecting your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting moments of laughter and describes an inability to find things funny, aligning with 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment in most activities and only minimal anticipation for two routine tasks, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('more often than I want to admit') and provides a detailed example, matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries about the baby's safety with looping thoughts lasting hours, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling "swallowed" and wondering "How am I going to get through today?" indicating most of the time she hasn't been able to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the day, almost every day," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week, clearly linked to feeling unhappy, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the EPDS falls well above the 14-point cut-off that signals probable major depression; endorsement of item 10 indicates presence of self-harm ideation. The constellation of <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>marked loss of interest</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>recurrent anxiety and panic</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and <sym>feelings of overwhelm</sym> lasting most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring anxiety features. <quote>I just want the heaviness to stop</quote> underscores intensity and distress. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Bring a trusted adult to the appointment and share the EPDS results openly so support is in place
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or your local emergency number if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Consider medication review-many antidepressants are compatible with breastfeeding and can bring rapid relief
5. Begin daily 20-minute outdoor walks and balanced meals to gently support mood and energy
6. Schedule brief respite breaks: let a partner, family member, or friend handle one night feeding or household block so you can rest
7. Join a local or virtual new-mother support group to reduce isolation and normalize professional help-seeking
8. Track mood, sleep, and anxiety levels daily to review with your clinician at follow-up visits
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
ID: Patient is 4–6 weeks post-delivery, breastfeeding, partnered, no PMH of mood disorders.

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Guilt / self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)  
- Excessive generalized anxiety, intrusive worries, panic-like episode (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, feeling “swallowed” by daily tasks (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia and middle-night wakening linked to ruminative worry (Q7)  
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation without plan or intent (Q10)

Pattern  
Symptoms present most days, interfere with sleep and basic coping, reported for ≥2 weeks. No current mania, psychosis, or substance use noted.

Screening significance  
High likelihood of major depressive episode with peripartum onset; co-occurring anxiety disorder/panic features cannot be ruled out. Passive SI detected → acute safety risk.

Risk factors identified  
- Daily sadness, anhedonia, guilt, crying spells  
- Mood-related insomnia  
- Overwhelm / difficulty coping  
- Passive SI (no intent/plan)

Next step  
Recommend immediate comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and safety planning; consider Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale for quantification; involve support person and provide 24-h crisis resources.
